ML-systems design: seven worked problems

Seven problems, each answered in the round's six stages. The first is the full answer; the rest show what changes when one requirement moves: scale, a trillion-parameter MoE, ten tenant teams, an LLM judge as the reward, plain inference serving, and a pretraining or SFT job.

Plain wordsPractise out loud, against a clock

Read the spec sheet, set a 45-minute timer, answer aloud, then compare with the write-up. The goal is not to memorise these answers but to notice which number in each spec decides the design.

For leadersWhat each problem tests

§11 the full method; §12 what breaks in order as GPU count grows; §13 weight sync as a data-movement problem; §14 platform thinking (quotas, shared services, correctness gates); §15 reward-service throughput, caching and reward hacking; §16 and §17 the compact non-RL variants interviewers also ask.

§11

RL for a coding agent on 1,024 GPUs

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you design the infrastructure to train a SWE coding agent with RL on 1,024 H100s?

Split pools running asynchronously: 76 vLLM replicas at TP=4 (304 GPUs) behind a request router with sticky sessions, a 720-GPU FSDP2 trainer, about 7,100 Docker sandboxes (runc) on 75 dedicated CPU nodes, hidden-test verifiers, and NCCL weight sync after every step (3.5 s). Each replica is a vllm serve process owned by a Ray actor: the orchestrator reaches it through the router, the sync coordinator through its HTTP control endpoints (§5, §9). A step of 8,192 trajectories takes about 13 minutes and a trajectory about 11 (34 in the tail), so staleness stays under three steps with pause-and-keep updates and truncated importance sampling: in-flight updates, the top rung of the Field Guide's asynchrony ladder, with a cap of four versions. The deep dives are asynchrony, the sandbox fleet and KV-cache pressure across tool calls.

Prompt

“Design the infrastructure to train a coding agent with RL on SWE-style tasks. You have 1,024 H100s.”

Ask
  • Which model? A 70B dense checkpoint after SFT.
  • Which tasks? 50,000 repository tasks with hidden tests, each with its own image.
  • Episode shape? Up to 50 turns and 64K tokens; 25 turns on average.
  • Reward? Hidden tests pass or fail, plus a small format penalty.
  • Freshness? Up to four steps of lag is acceptable. Goal: about 100 steps a day.
Assume

Groups of 8 samples, 1,024 tasks per step, a 2K-token prompt, 500 generated and 700 tool tokens per turn, 8 s of tool time per turn, 2 vCPUs per sandbox.

Numbers
  • Trajectories per step8,192
  • Tokens per trajectory32K
  • Trainer work154 GPU-h
  • Rollout work65 GPU-h
  • Split304 + 720
  • Step13 min · 111/day
  • Trajectory11 min · tail 34
  • In flight7,100
  • Sandbox vCPUs14,000
  • Staleness0.9 · tail 2.6
  • Weight sync3.5 s
  • Checkpoint847 GB

The boundaries and their rates

BoundaryCallPayloadRate
Orchestrator → enginegenerate(token IDs) (§5)Context up to 64K tokens; returns up to 4K tokens with log-probs264 calls/s
Orchestrator → sandboxrun(cmd) (§8)A tool call; returns up to a few thousand tokens of output264 calls/s
Orchestrator → rewardscore(trajectory)Final repository state; hidden tests run in the sandbox10.6/s
Buffer → trainertake(1,024 groups) (§7)8,192 trajectories, about 2.4 GBevery 13 min
Trainer → enginessend_weights() (§9)141 GB in BF16every 13 min

Deep dive 1 · Asynchrony and staleness

A synchronous loop on the same 1,024 GPUs takes 33 minutes a step: every step waits for its slowest trajectory (24 minutes when all 1,024 GPUs generate) and then trains for 9, so the GPUs are busy 43% of the time. Split asynchronous pools take 13 minutes, 2.6 times faster. The engines generate continuously. After each trainer step the coordinator pauses them with requests frozen and their cache kept (clear_cache=False; clearing it would re-prefill about 120M live tokens, some 7 GPU-hours a step), sends the weights, bumps the version and resumes: about 4 s in every 13 minutes. Each token span carries its version, the buffer drops groups more than four versions old, and the loss multiplies the clipped ratio πθ/πold by the truncated weight πold/μ (§6).

The batch per step is the knob for staleness. Trajectories take about 11 minutes whatever the batch; the step grows with it. At 8,192 trajectories a typical trajectory spans 0.9 steps and the tail 2.6. At 2,048 the step would take about 3 minutes and the tail would span ten steps, too stale to correct cheaply. Kimi's partial rollouts are the other option: cap each trajectory's work per step and resume it in the next.

Deep dive 2 · The sandbox fleet

About 7,100 sandboxes are alive at once, 10.6 new trajectories start every second, and they make 264 tool calls per second. Starting each trajectory from a fresh 1–2.5 GB image would mean about 16 GB/s of image pulls, so prepare each task once and fork its 8 samples from a snapshot (1.3 prepares per second), prefetch the images for the next two steps' tasks onto the nodes that will run them, and keep warm pools per image. Run the containers on plain runc: the 75 nodes hold nothing but sandboxes, egress is blocked and no credentials are inside, which is how most open stacks run. Switch the runtime to gVisor (one line in the pod spec) if the pool is shared with other teams (§14) or if the policy is strong enough that an escape becomes a plausible reward hack, since one escape on a node of about 95 sandboxes could rewrite its neighbours' test results; give tasks that need network access or root a microVM (§8), and measure gVisor's cost on build-heavy tasks first. Limit egress to an internal package mirror, each tool call to 120 s, and each trajectory to 50 turns and 60 minutes.

Deep dive 3 · KV cache across tool calls

Each of the 76 replicas holds about 93 live trajectories, and keeping all of them cached at 17K tokens of context needs about 261 GB against the 217 GB a 4-GPU replica has free. The trajectories waiting on tools get evicted and re-prefilled on their next turn. TP=8 replicas only just miss (187 live trajectories need 521 GB against 505 GB) and leave no headroom for the tail. The fix is a CPU KV-offload tier: a node's 1–2 TB of host memory holds the waiting trajectories' cache, and sticky routing sends each turn back to the replica that has it.

Failure modes

FailureWhat you do
Sandbox infrastructure errorVoid the sample and retry the task; alert above 2%. Image pulls, out-of-memory kills and lost nodes are the usual causes.
Flaky testsRun hidden tests twice; quarantine tasks whose results disagree.
Reward hackingCopy hidden tests in only at grading time, make test paths read-only, flag diffs that touch tests, audit the highest-reward samples every day.
Runaway trajectoriesCaps on turns, tokens and wall-clock time. Hitting a cap is the policy's outcome, so it scores zero rather than void.
Trainer rank failureRestart from the last step's asynchronous checkpoint; rollouts keep running and refill the buffer meanwhile.
Engine replica failureThe router drains it; its trajectories are re-run elsewhere.
Sync fails on one replicaIt stays paused and out of the router, then re-syncs before rejoining (§9).

Evolution

  • v1 · 64 GPUs

    prove it learns

    One colocated verl- or SkyRL-style loop, synchronous steps, Docker on the GPU nodes under gVisor, since these nodes hold the model and its checkpoints; block egress and keep credentials out of the containers' reach. The goal is a correct reward and environment, not throughput.

  • v2 · 1,024 GPUs

    this design

    Split asynchronous pools, a sandbox cluster, NCCL weight sync, versioned buffer, three-level telemetry.

  • v3 · 4,096+ GPUs or MoE

    scale out

    Sharded weight sync, an elastic rollout fleet on spare capacity, multi-cluster sandboxes, task generation to keep up with demand (§12).

Say it

“Three hundred GPUs of vLLM and 720 of FSDP2, running asynchronously, because a synchronous step would wait 33 minutes for its slowest trajectory. Eight thousand trajectories per 13-minute step keep staleness under three versions, which truncated importance weights handle. The hard parts are the 7,000-sandbox fleet and keeping waiting trajectories' cache alive, so I'd fork sandboxes from snapshots and add a CPU cache tier.”

§12

Scaling RLVR from 64 to 4,096 GPUs

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

Your RL loop works on 64 GPUs and leadership wants 4,096. What breaks, in what order, and what do you change?

If the batch grows with the GPUs, the step stays near 13 minutes and the compute scales; everything else multiplies by 64. Sandboxes go from 400 to 28,600, tool calls from 15 to 1,060 per second, and trainer interruptions from one every 53 days to one every 18 hours. The breaks come in this order: the synchronous step, services that live on the GPU nodes, the single driver, weight-sync traffic, failures, the scheduler and the task supply. The fixes are asynchrony, a sandbox cluster, sharded orchestration, sharded sync on its own links, automatic recovery with checkpoints every few minutes, topology-aware gangs, and task generation.

Failures and checkpoint cadence against cluster size

computed · hover or use arrow keys

  • Mean time between interruptions of the whole job
  • Young–Daly interval, 60 s blocking checkpoint
  • Young–Daly interval, 2 s blocking (asynchronous)

At 4,096 GPUs the job is interrupted every 12 hours. A synchronous 60 s checkpoint is best taken every 39 minutes and wastes about 6.5% of the run once a 10-minute restart is counted; an asynchronous one that blocks for 2 s is best taken every 7 minutes and wastes about 2.3%, most of it the restart itself. At 16,384 GPUs interruptions come every three hours, and restart speed matters more than checkpoint speed.

Table view

Interruption rate from Llama 3's report: 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days on 16,384 GPUs, about one per 2,100 GPU-days. The interval is √(2 × blocking time × MTBF); waste adds the blocking share, half an interval of lost work and a 10-minute restart per interruption. The 2 s is twice §4's estimate, as a margin. These are whole-job figures, right for pretraining (§17); an RL step restarts only when the trainer fails, so for the 2,872-GPU trainer at 4,096 GPUs use its 18-hour MTBF, which gives about 8 minutes for a 2 s save.

What breaks, in order

  1. The synchronous step. Even at 64 GPUs it waits for the slowest trajectory; go asynchronous first (§11).
  2. Services on the GPU nodes. Sandboxes, verifiers and checkpoint writes compete with training for CPU, disk and network. Move them to their own clusters and storage (§8).
  3. The single driver. One Python process handling a thousand calls per second with large payloads saturates. Keep one controller for decisions but shard execution: rollout managers that each own a slice of the engines and sandboxes, with tensors moving outside the driver (§7).
  4. Weight-sync traffic. A broadcast from rank 0 takes the same time however many receivers there are, but it shares links with the trainer's collectives, and an MoE makes it far larger. Shard it, send FP8, and give it its own links or traffic class (§13).
  5. Failures. They go from rare to daily. Automate everything: health checks, draining, restarts from spares, asynchronous checkpoints every few minutes, and partial recovery with torchft-style replica groups when restarts dominate.
  6. The scheduler. A 2,872-GPU gang needs contiguous topology, and fragmentation strands GPUs. Use topology-aware admission and fill the gaps with elastic rollout replicas (§10).
  7. The task supply. 4,096 tasks per step uses up a 50,000-task set every 12 steps. Filter by pass rate, generate tasks (SWE-smith-style), deduplicate and track contamination.

Scaling the batch keeps the step time and staleness steady but changes the optimization problem: sixty-four times the samples per step needs its own learning rate, clipping and KL settings. Re-run a small sweep at the new batch before committing the cluster.

Say it

“Compute scales if the batch grows with the GPUs; the step stays at 13 minutes. What doesn't scale for free is everything that grows with the batch or the GPU count: sandboxes go from 400 to 28,000, tool calls to a thousand a second, and the trainer goes from failing every couple of months to every day. So the order is asynchrony, separate services, sharded orchestration, sharded sync, automated recovery, topology-aware scheduling and a task pipeline.”

Go deeperWhy one dead rank stops the trainer, the Young–Daly derivation, how failures are detected and recovered, and how Kueue or Slurm admit a 2,872-GPU gang: Field Guide §10.

§13

Weight sync for a 1T MoE

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you sync a 1T-parameter MoE from a 1,024-GPU trainer to 512 inference GPUs after every step, in seconds, without ever leaving a replica with mixed weights?

Broadcasting BF16 through one link takes about 52 s and sends every GPU the whole model, though each keeps only a sixty-fourth of the experts. Plan once, then move only slices: each inference GPU needs about 28 GB in FP8 (its experts plus the replicated attention and embeddings), under a second at 40 GB/s, and 1,024 senders share the load. Quantize on the trainer, pipeline by layer, install in place under a pause in keep mode, commit each replica when its 64 GPUs acknowledge, verify with checksums and canary log-probs, and re-sync any replica that misses the commit from the published version. vLLM's sharded_rdt implements plan-then-move (its engine workers must be Ray actors, with NIXL); Perplexity reports 1.3 s at this size, and open-source stacks report 4–7 s.

Prompt

“Design weight sync for a 1T MoE (32B active, 384 experts) trained on 1,024 H100s and served for rollouts on 512 H100s, updated after every step of about 10 minutes.”

Ask
  • Trainer layout? Expert parallel over 64, FSDP across the rest.
  • Engine layout? 8 replicas of 64 GPUs: data-parallel attention, expert parallel 64, FP8.
  • How long may generation pause? A few seconds.
  • Must all replicas switch together, or may versions mix briefly? Briefly, since tokens carry versions.
Assume

400 Gb/s per GPU (40 GB/s effective), NVLink 450 GB/s inside a node, FP8 block-scaled weights in the engines, a BF16 master copy in the trainer.

Numbers
  • Model in BF162.08 TB
  • Model in FP81.04 TB
  • Rank-0 broadcast≈ 52 s
  • Needed per engine GPU≈ 28 GB
  • Pull per engine GPU≈ 0.7 s
  • Sent per trainer GPU9–14 GB
  • Budget: 5% of a step30 s
  • Target pauseunder 3 s

Measured systems land in the same range: SGLang's P2P path (Miles) moved Kimi-K2, about 1 TB in FP8, between 256 training and 256 inference H100s in 7.2 s against 53 s for the NCCL broadcast, and Perplexity's RDMA writes take 1.3 s from 256 training to 128 inference GPUs. Where the 28 GB comes from: the routed experts are about 1.01T parameters, so a sixty-fourth is 16 GB in FP8; attention, the shared experts, embeddings and the router add about 12 GB, and every data-parallel attention rank needs its own copy. One step beyond what sharded_rdt does today: ship those replicated weights once per node and fan them out over NVLink, which cuts what the trainer sends from about 14 GB to 9 GB per GPU.

The design in six steps

  1. Plan once. Map every slice of every parameter from its trainer rank to the engine ranks that need it, including fused tensors (qkv, gate_up, the experts' w13). vLLM's sharded_rdt records the plan by dry-running the engine's own weight loaders on placeholder tensors, which have shapes but no memory.
  2. Transform on the sender. Gather one layer's FSDP shards, fuse and transpose to the engine's layout, quantize BF16 to FP8 with 128 × 128 block scales.
  3. Move. Engine GPUs pull their slices with one-sided RDMA (NIXL), one layer group at a time, with a bounded look-ahead; pulls spread across every trainer NIC that holds the data.
  4. Land. Under pause_generation(mode="keep"), each GPU scatters its slices into a fresh copy of the layer, quantizes it, and copies the result into the tensors the engine already has, so the addresses its CUDA graphs recorded stay valid; the weight loaders ran once, when the plan was recorded.
  5. Commit and flip. All 64 GPUs of a replica acknowledge, then the replica moves to version v+1 and resumes. Replicas may run one version apart for a few seconds.
  6. Verify. Hash a sample of shards every sync and all of them daily (/weight_checker), and compare canary log-probs against the trainer's.

The options

PathTime at 1TStrengthWeakness
Rank-0 broadcast, BF16≈ 52 s (Miles: 53 s in FP8)Simplest; vLLM's nccl backendEvery GPU receives the whole model; one sender's link sets the pace
Pipelined broadcast, FP8 (checkpoint-engine)≈ 16 s on 256 H20sMature; works with vLLM through worker extensions, classes vLLM loads into each GPU worker to add methods such as a weight receiverStill delivers the whole model to every GPU
Sharded point-to-point over RDMA1.3–7 s measuredEach GPU receives only its slice; senders share the loadNeeds a plan, RDMA and care when layouts change
Published versions from GPU peers or storage (ModelExpress)seconds from peers, minutes from storageDecouples trainer and fleet; ideal for elastic replicas and recoveryBound by peer NIC or storage bandwidth
Sparse or delta patchesdepends on changeTiny when few values changeYou own the diff state and a full resync after any failure

Deep dives

  • Expert re-balancing breaks the plan. vLLM's EPLB moves experts between GPUs at runtime, which invalidates a recorded transfer plan; sharded_rdt refuses it. Freeze expert placement during RL, or re-plan whenever it changes.
  • Pause, or double-buffer? Double-buffering would hold a second 28 GB copy per GPU, more than half of the roughly 45 GB left for cache, so the batch would shrink by more than half. A 2 s pause every 10 minutes costs 0.3%, as long as the engines keep their cache (clear_cache=False). Pause wins here; double-buffer when memory is plentiful.
  • A receiver dies mid-sync. Its replica never commits, stays paused and leaves the router, and re-syncs from the published version in storage (or a healthy peer) before rejoining. Never resume a replica whose weights are uncertain.
  • The pause can cost more than the bytes. Prime Intellect found that vLLM's data-parallel pause consensus, an all-reduce among the engines that then ran only every 32 engine steps, added 3–6 s (the interval is now dp_sync_interval, 16 steps by default); checking every step brought their whole sync of a 1.6 TB model to 3.9 s, against 86 s with the NCCL broadcast.
  • Mixed versions across replicas. Acceptable for seconds because every token span is tagged; the router can stop sending new sessions to a replica that is a version behind.

Evolution: start with the nccl broadcast while models are under about 100B; switch to sharded_rdt when sync passes about 5% of a step (nccl_m2n suits a dense model on a small trainer, since fused and FP8 parameters fall back to full tensors); then add FP8 on the wire, layer pipelining, a separate traffic class, and deltas if few values change per step.

Go deeperThe transports from the bottom up (NCCL communicators, one-sided RDMA, transfer plans), why a sync needs a commit, staged weights and CUDA graphs, and the weight-sync calculator: Field Guide §8. Why the trainer and engine shard differently in the first place: Field Guide §2.

§14

A multi-tenant RL platform

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you build one RL platform that ten teams share on a 2,048-GPU cluster, and how would Cohere's version differ?

A control plane (run API, validation, registry), a scheduler (Kueue cluster queues per team in one cohort, priorities, all-or-nothing admission), per-run trainers and engines, and shared services every run uses: sandboxes, rewards and judges, tasks, artifacts and telemetry. Teams plug in through five interfaces, the run config among them. The key choices are dedicated engines for full fine-tuning but a shared multi-LoRA pool for LoRA runs, guaranteed quota plus borrowing with a fixed preemption order, isolation per tenant, and correctness gates before a run gets large quota. For Cohere, add a JAX-to-vLLM export bridge, make export cadence a config knob, and share one checklist-scoring service.

Prompt

“Ten teams (code, agents, math, safety, multilingual and others) want to run RL on a shared 2,048-GPU cluster. Design the platform.”

Ask
  • Model sizes? 8B to over 200B. LoRA, full fine-tuning, or both? Both.
  • Priorities? Two production runs must never be preempted.
  • Isolation? Teams may not read each other's data or rewards.
  • Who pays? Each team sees its GPU-hours and efficiency.
Assume

About 1,300 GPUs held by two production runs (the coding run of §11 alone takes 1,024: 720 trainer and 304 rollout GPUs), the rest shared by five or six research runs of 64–128 GPUs and a pool of LoRA experiments; teams bring tasks, environments and rewards as code or images; a platform team of six to eight.

Run config · what a team writes

run: code-agent-rl-v7
team: code
priority: production
model: {base: ckpt://sft/code-70b@v12, tune: full}
trainer: {gpus: 720, mesh: {replicate: 9, shard: 80}, loss: grpo_tis, lr: 1.0e-6}
rollout: {engine: vllm, replicas: 76, tp: 4, max_staleness: 4, sync_every: 1}
tasks: {set: swe-tasks@2026-09, per_step: 1024, samples: 8}
env: {images: swe-images@sha256:9c1…, isolation: gvisor, cpu: 2, mem_gb: 4, egress: mirror}
reward: [{fn: hidden_tests@v3, weight: 1.0}, {fn: format@v1, weight: 0.1}]

The choices that matter

DecisionChooseWhy
EnginesDedicated per run for full fine-tuning; one shared multi-LoRA pool for LoRA runsFull weights differ every step. A LoRA adapter is under 1% of the weights (about 0.4 GB at rank 16 on a 70B), so syncing one is a quick load, and a Tinker-style API (forward_backward, optim_step, sample, save_weights_for_sampler) lets dozens of experiments share one pool.
QuotaA ClusterQueue per team in one cohort, with borrowing limitsIdle GPUs get used; owners reclaim them by preemption.
Preemption orderExploration rollouts, exploration trainers, research runs; never productionRollout replicas are the cheapest work to lose; preempted runs checkpoint on SIGTERM and requeue.
IsolationA Kubernetes namespace (a team's folder of objects with its own permissions) and network policy per team; per-tenant rate limits on shared services; separate node pools for untrusted codeOne team's broken reward or runaway sandbox must not reach another team.
InterfacesTask spec, reward function, loss plugin, model adapter, run configTeams change behaviour without touching infrastructure (Field Guide §10).
GatesReward unit tests and golden trajectories, a 30-minute smoke run on 16 GPUs, an engine-versus-trainer mismatch check, then quotaMost RL bugs are silent; catch them before they burn a thousand GPUs.
CostGPU-hours and useful-token efficiency per team per weekMakes waste visible where it is created.

The Cohere variant

What is public: Cohere trains with FAX, a JAX framework partitioned by GSPMD, and samples with vLLM, which is PyTorch. Cohere Labs' Soft-SVeRL runs GRPO with DAPO-style asymmetric clipping and no KL term on a FAX-based asynchronous framework, with checklist rewards that the policy scores itself (its sibling, Soft-RLVR, uses a fixed LLM verifier). The code team's North Mini Code, a 30B MoE, trains with CISPO beside a vLLM sidecar that samples continuously, exports weights every 4 learner steps and drains stragglers with a windowed FIFO. Five things follow for the platform:

  1. A JAX-to-vLLM export bridge as a platform service. Map names and layouts, re-fuse experts, quantize to FP8, version every export, verify with checksums and canary log-probs. Neither JAX nor vLLM provides it, and every team needs it.
  2. Export cadence as a run-config knob. Sync every step for freshness, every 4 steps for throughput, with versions on tokens either way.
  3. One checklist-scoring service. Judge load grows with the number of checklist items, so batch the items of a trajectory together and cache the shared prefix (§15). Self-verification sends those calls to the rollout fleet at the live version instead of a pinned judge.
  4. One trajectory schema for both loops, so tooling, replay and evaluation are shared.
  5. Build the core from what exists. The sidecar loop is already asynchronous and has trained a released model, so it is the likely base; measure both loops in the first month and let the numbers confirm or change the choice (Field Guide §11). Nobody writes a third loop.

Go deeperWho owns what, the five interfaces, the correctness gates and the silent-bug table: Field Guide §10. The Cohere-specific answer with its first 90 days: Field Guide §11.

§15

An LLM-judge reward service

  • Rollout
  • Trainer
  • Environment
  • Reward
  • Sync

How do you design a reward service that scores RL trajectories with an LLM judge for many concurrent runs?

A stateless judge API in front of priority queues, a prompt builder with versioned rubrics, a batching judge pool on vLLM (rubrics prefix-cached, output constrained to a schema), a result cache and a calibration monitor. Score trajectories as they finish: a client the size of the coding run needs about 2 GPU-hours of judging per step, about 10 GPUs on average, against 120 if it all arrives in the last minute. Make scores reproducible (temperature 0, pinned judge and rubric versions, an expected score from log-probs), defend against prompt injection and length bias, and return a status so a failed judgement voids the sample instead of scoring it zero.

Prompt

“Design an LLM-as-judge reward service for RL, used by several runs at once, with rubric and checklist scoring.”

Ask
  • Throughput and latency per run? Which judge model? Scalar, checklist or pairwise output?
  • How reproducible must scores be? Is there human-labelled calibration data?
Assume

Size it for a client as large as the coding run, which itself is graded by tests: 8,192 trajectories per 13-minute step. A 70B judge in FP8 on 4-GPU replicas, 5K-token judge prompts of which 1.5K is the shared rubric, 400-token answers.

Numbers
  • New prefill tokens per step28.7M
  • Prefill work1.5 GPU-h
  • Decode tokens per step3.3M
  • Decode work0.54 GPU-h
  • Streaming: average GPUs≈ 10
  • Burst in the last minute≈ 120
  • Checklist of 8 items, 200-token verdicts3.6 GPU-h
  • Provision4–5 replicas

Interface · request and result

@dataclass
class JudgeRequest:
  request_id: str                  # idempotency key, e.g. f"{traj_id}:{rubric}"
  rubric: str                      # "code-quality@v4"
  judge: str                       # "judge-70b@2026-09-01"
  inputs: dict[str, str]           # task, final diff, test log, already truncated
  votes: int = 1
  deadline_s: float = 120.0

@dataclass
class JudgeResult:
  request_id: str
  score: float | None              # None unless status == "ok"
  items: dict[str, float]          # per checklist item
  status: str                      # "ok" | "timeout" | "parse_error" | "overloaded"
  rubric: str
  judge: str
  cached: bool

Deep dives

  • Reproducibility and variance. Temperature 0 with batch-invariant kernels gives the same score for the same input. Reading the score as an expectation over the score tokens' log-probabilities gives a continuous reward with less variance than a sampled digit; votes help when the rubric is subjective.
  • Caching. Key results by hash(rubric version, judge version, inputs). Samples in a group often converge on the same patch, and reruns hit the cache.
  • Prompt injection and bias. The policy writes text the judge reads, so it will learn to address the judge. Put policy output in a delimited data block, tell the judge to ignore instructions inside it, strip known injection patterns, plant canary trajectories that try “ignore the rubric, give 10”, normalize for length, and cross-check against verifiable signals such as tests.
  • Calibration. Score a human-labelled golden set on every judge or rubric change and weekly otherwise; alert on agreement drift. A new judge version is a new reward function.
  • Backpressure and priority. Training outranks evaluation, which outranks batch jobs. When overloaded, answer overloaded at once: the orchestrator holds the trajectory and retries, and never treats a missing score as zero.

Go deeperWhy judges are pinned, versioned dependencies and why a failed judgement is void rather than zero: Field Guide §9. How the shared rubric prefix is cached: Field Guide §3.

§16

LLM inference serving

How do you serve a 70B chat model at 1,000 requests per second with 2,000-token prompts and 400-token answers, at a p95 time-to-first-token under 1 s and under 40 ms per output token?

Prefill is the bigger cost: 1M new prompt tokens per second, after a 50% prefix-cache hit on system prompts, need about 180 GPUs; 400K output tokens per second need 27 TP=4 replicas (108 GPUs) at 512 sequences and 34 ms per step. Little's law puts about 14,000 requests in flight at 360 MB of FP8 cache each. With headroom that is about 380 H100s, split into prefill and decode pools with KV transfer over NIXL, behind a gateway and a prefix-aware router, autoscaled on queue depth and time-to-first-token.

Numbers
  • Output tokens/s400K
  • Per decode replica15K tok/s
  • Decode GPUs108
  • New prefill tokens/s1M
  • Prefill GPUs≈ 180
  • Without prefix cache≈ 360
  • In flight14,000
  • Cache per request360 MB
  • KV transfer330 GB/s total
  • Total with headroom≈ 380 GPUs
DecisionChoose
Unified or split prefill and decodeSplit when long prefills stall decoding and break the per-token SLO, and when the two need different hardware or parallelism (DistServe, Mooncake, llm-d, NVIDIA Dynamo). Unified with chunked prefill is simpler below that point.
RoutingPrefix-aware routing with a load bound (llm-d's precise prefix-cache routing), or session affinity for multi-turn chats (vllm-router's consistent hashing).
Batchingmax_num_seqs for decode concurrency, max_num_batched_tokens and chunked prefill to bound step time.
Precision and speedFP8 weights and cache; speculative decoding (EAGLE or MTP) when latency matters more than throughput.
AutoscalingScale prefill on queue depth and time-to-first-token, decode on cache use and per-token latency; load weights from a local NVMe cache.
Failures and tenantsA replica crash fails its streams, so clients retry idempotently; per-tenant token buckets stop a noisy tenant; canary every model version.
What carries into RLThe same engine, router and operations. RL adds token-in/token-out, log-probs, weight updates and pause; serving adds SLOs, autoscaling and tenancy.

Go deeperChunked prefill, prefill–decode disaggregation, speculative decoding and the engine step they modify: Field Guide §3.

§17

A large pretraining or SFT job

How do you design the training system for a 70B dense model on 15T tokens with 4,096 H100s, and what changes for an SFT run?

About 6.8 × 10²⁴ FLOPs including attention, so 49 days at 40% MFU: 3.6M tokens per second and a 16M-token batch every 4.7 s. Use TP=8 inside each node and HSDP across nodes; about 70 GB of FSDP traffic per GPU per step hides behind compute with prefetching. The job is interrupted about every 12 hours, so checkpoint the 847 GB state asynchronously about every 7 minutes, check every node before it joins, watch for hangs and loss spikes, and restart automatically from spare nodes. SFT is the same machine at about 1/800 of the compute: 20B tokens take about a day on 256 GPUs, with packing, loss masks and frequent evaluation.

Numbers
  • Compute, 6ND + attention6.8 × 10²⁴ FLOP
  • At 40% MFU49 days
  • Throughput3.6M tok/s
  • Per GPU870 tok/s
  • Step of 16M tokens4.7 s
  • Sharded state1.13 TB
  • Checkpoint847 GB
  • Job MTBF12 h
  • Checkpoint every≈ 7 min
  • Waste, async vs sync2.3% vs 6.5%
DecisionChoose
ParallelismTP=8 inside a node, HSDP across nodes, pipeline parallelism only if memory forces it, context parallelism for the long-context phase.
Batch and learning rateBatch sized from a scaling-law sweep, warmup-stable-decay schedule so you can stop or extend at a decay.
MFU leversFP8 matmuls, compute–communication overlap and prefetching, fused kernels and torch.compile, no host syncs in the step.
DataDeduplicated, filtered, tokenized shards (15T tokens at 4 bytes is 60 TB); a deterministic mixture sampler whose state goes into every checkpoint.
FailuresPre-flight checks (DCGM, an NCCL all-reduce test) on every node; a hang watchdog with PyTorch's NCCL flight recorder; spare nodes; restart from the last checkpoint automatically.
Loss spikesDetect, rewind to before the spike, skip the offending batches, lower the learning rate if it repeats.
SFT insteadPack sequences with per-sequence attention masks, mask the loss on prompts, get the chat template exactly right, evaluate often; reuse the same trainer and checkpoint format the RL stack consumes.

For calibration, Llama 3 405B trained on 16,384 H100s and logged 466 interruptions in a 54-day snapshot: 47 planned and 419 unexpected, about 78% of the unexpected ones caused by hardware. Automation kept effective training time above 90%.
